FOR GUTTER CLEANING CONTRACTORS

Bid the stories and the downspouts, not the linear feet.

Price a gutter cleaning the way the job actually takes time: each run of trough, the story it sits on, the pitch, whether guards are in the way, what is in it, and every downspout you have to flush. You get the visit price, what that works out to per linear foot, the walk-away number, and an optional spring-and-fall contract.

New to two-story pricing? Why a second story is not twice the footage. Already run field service software? How this calculator differs from Jobber. Bidding by the foot? This calculator vs. a flat price per linear foot.

The house

One row per distinct run. A 40-foot two-story rear is a different job from 40 feet of one-story garage screens — putting them on the same per-foot price is how a cheap quote loses money.

Where the labor goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting minutes and difficulty factors are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    What does this gutter cleaning estimate include?

    The visit price adds up loaded labor for every run you enter — linear feet, downspout flushing, and travel/setup — plus disposal, equipment, overhead, and your target margin, then applies a minimum stop charge if the raw price comes in under it. Nothing is a flat per-linear-foot rate.

    Why do story, pitch, guards, and debris all multiply together?

    Each run's difficulty factor is story × pitch × guards × debris, all against a one-story, low-pitch, open-gutter, leaf-only baseline. A two-story steep-pitch run behind micro-mesh screens clogged with needles can take several times longer per foot than that baseline — a flat per-foot quote cannot see that difference, which is exactly how it loses money.

    Why do downspouts only inherit the story factor, not pitch, guards, or debris?

    Flushing and testing a downspout is a separate task from clearing the trough. Pitch, guards, and debris change how hard the trough itself is to clear, so they don't apply to the downspout line — but a second-story leader still takes longer to reach and test, so the story factor does.

    What's the difference between a one-time visit and a seasonal contract?

    Visits per year controls this: 1 prices a single clean, and 2 or more multiplies that same visit price by the number of cleanings — typically a spring-and-fall contract — for the annual total shown at the bottom of the bid. Each visit is priced identically; the tool doesn't discount repeat visits on its own.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. “Copy share link” encodes your runs and cost inputs into this page's own URL hash so a partner or the office can open the same bid; nothing is sent to a server. Only your business name and contact details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser's local storage, and “Forget my business details” clears them.

    Does this check gutter damage, roof condition, or drainage?

    No. Hours and difficulty factors are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a roof or drainage inspection. Cleaning clears debris; it says nothing about sagging fascia, failing seams, undersized downspouts, or whether the runoff actually drains once it leaves them — that's a judgment call for the site visit, and the printed proposal says so too.

two-story-gutter-cleaning-cost.html.text:
← Gutter cleaning bid calculator

Why two-story gutter cleaning costs more than twice the footage

Homeowners compare quotes on linear feet. Contractors who price that way lose the two-story jobs and overcharge the ranches. The trough length is the same; the minutes are not.

The second story is a labor multiplier, not more pipe

On a one-story eave a crew can walk most of the run from a single ladder set, or from the roof if the pitch is low. On a two-story eave every section is a new set, a longer carry, and a slower clean because one hand is managing reach and the other is scooping. A useful starting multiplier is about 1.6× on the one-story baseline — not 2×, because the trough itself did not get longer, and not 1×, because the access did.

Steep pitch stacks on top of that. Guards stack on top of that. Pine needles stack on top of that. A 40-foot two-story micro-mesh run in fir needles is a different job from 40 feet of open one-story leaf trough, even though both are “40 linear feet.”

Downspouts are a separate job

Flushing and testing a leader is not included in a per-foot trough rate. Each downspout is minutes of its own, and a second-story leader takes longer to reach and confirm. A house with six downspouts and short eaves can take as long as a house with long eaves and two.

Gutter guards do not make the visit cheaper

Screens and micro-mesh reduce how often a house needs service. They increase the time of the visit that still has to happen, because debris is under or in the covering. Price the visit you are actually doing. If guards mean the house is now once a year instead of twice, that shows up as visits-per-year, not as a discount on the hour.

Quote the visit, then look at the implied foot price

The number a contractor should hold is the visit price that covers loaded labor, travel, disposal, overhead, and the margin they mean to keep — and the walk-away number below it. The implied dollars per linear foot is a sanity check, not the bid. The gutter cleaning bid calculator does that arithmetic from your own crew times. The starting multipliers are ballpark figures, not a standard.

Common questions

Why does two-story gutter cleaning cost more than the extra linear feet?

A second story adds ladder moves, reach time, and a safety tax on every foot. The trough is the same length, but the minutes per foot are not. A common starting multiplier is about 1.6× for two stories on top of the one-story baseline, before pitch, guards, or debris.

Do gutter guards make cleaning cheaper?

No. Screens and especially micro-mesh slow a clean because debris has to be lifted out of or pulled through the covering. Guards reduce how often a house needs service; they do not reduce the time of the visit that still has to happen.

Should I quote gutter cleaning per linear foot?

Use linear feet as an input, not as the price. Two houses with the same footage can differ by more than 2× in labor once stories, pitch, guards, pine needles, and downspouts are counted. Quote the visit, then look at the implied dollars per foot as a sanity check.

vs-a-flat-price-per-linear-foot.html.text:
← Gutter Cleaning Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per linear foot

Gutter companies are told to bid by the linear foot. That rule cannot see the house — stories, pitch, guards, and debris change the minutes per foot, and two houses of identical footage can differ by nearly five times in labor.

What a flat price per linear foot is

A price per linear foot is the fastest number to quote over the phone: pace off the trough, multiply by a rate, read back a total. It is also the unit customers already compare between competing postcards.

The rate behind it was learned from a specific house — a given story count, roof pitch, guard type, and debris load — and then reused for the next footage that calls in, whether or not that next house shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each gutter run's linear feet, story, roof pitch, guard type, debris load, and downspout count, plus your own wage, payroll burden, minutes per 10 feet, minutes per downspout, travel time, disposal, equipment, overhead, and target margin. It multiplies each run's minutes by its own story, pitch, guard, and debris factors, adds downspout flush time, and returns the visit price, the price per linear foot, the effective hourly rate, and an optional spring-and-fall contract total — for this house, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat per-foot rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a one-story ranch and a two-story house with the identical footage, even though a second story is extra ladder moves and reach time on every run. Multiplies each run's minutes by a story factor — 1, 1.5, 2, or 3 stories — so a taller house costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for gutter guards — open troughs and micro-mesh get the same rate, even though mesh turns a scoop into a pick. Prices open, screen, and micro-mesh guards as their own multiplier on top of the base minutes per foot.
Has no line for debris type or roof pitch — light leaves and packed pine needles on a steep roof get the same rate. Prices pitch and debris as their own multipliers, so a steep roof under conifers costs more than a walkable roof with light leaves.
Bills downspouts inside the same blended per-foot number, if at all. Prices each downspout's flush-and-test time separately, still scaled by story but not by pitch or guards — a second-story leader takes longer to reach, but a downspout is not harder to flush because the trough has mesh.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per linear foot and the effective hourly rate alongside the price, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same 150 feet, two different houses

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $22 blended wage, 30% burden, 8 minutes per 10 linear feet, 8 minutes per downspout, 20 minutes travel and setup, $15 disposal, $10 equipment, 15% overhead, 25% target margin, $125 minimum stop charge:

A 150-foot, one-story house with open gutters and light leaf debris (5 downspouts) takes 3.0 hours and prices at $169.89 for the visit — $1.13 per linear foot.

Pour the identical 150 feet onto a two-story house instead — moderate roof pitch, micro-mesh guards, pine-needle debris, the same 5 downspouts — and it takes 14.4 hours, costs $500.84 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $667.79 — $4.45 per linear foot. Quoting the two-story house at the ranch's learned rate of $1.13 per linear foot reproduces the ranch's price, $169.89, which is $330.95 below the two-story house's own break-even cost — before counting the $497.89 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 25% target margin. On a spring-and-fall contract, that gap doubles to $995.79 a year. Same 150 feet, same rate, one house that pays and one that loses money the moment the ladder goes up.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per linear foot get a gutter-cleaning bid wrong?

Because linear feet only measure the length of the run, not what it takes to clean it. A 150-foot, one-story house with open gutters and light leaf debris takes about 3.0 hours. The identical 150 feet on a two-story house with a moderate roof pitch, micro-mesh guards, and pine-needle debris takes about 14.4 hours -- almost five times the labor on the same footage, because story, pitch, guards, and debris each multiply the minutes per foot.

What does a flat per-foot rate usually miss entirely?

Story, pitch, guards, and debris, and the downspouts. A flat rate has no line for a second story slowing down every reach, no line for a steep or moderate pitch making the trough harder to work, no line for micro-mesh turning a scoop into a pick, and no line for pine needles taking longer to clear than loose leaves. It also has no separate line for downspout flushes, which still take longer on a second story even though the trough work is billed by the foot.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs: a 150-foot, one-story house with open gutters and leaves prices at $169.89 for the visit -- $1.13 per linear foot, on 3.0 hours of work. The identical 150 feet on a two-story house with micro-mesh guards and needle debris takes 14.4 hours, costs $500.84 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $667.79 -- $4.45 per linear foot. Quoting the harder house at the easier house's learned rate of $1.13 per linear foot reproduces the easier price, $169.89, which is $330.95 below the harder house's own break-even cost -- before counting the $497.89 it falls short of this calculator's price at a 25% target margin. On a spring-and-fall contract, that gap doubles to $995.79 a year.

Is a flat price per linear foot ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of similar houses -- one story, open gutters, light leaf debris -- a per-foot number can land close, because that is probably the house the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a two-story house, one with gutter guards, or one under pine or fir trees the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the story, the pitch, the guards, or the debris until someone is on the ladder, and by then the per-foot number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or disposal costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your dump fees. It takes each gutter run's linear feet, story, pitch, guard type, debris, and downspout count, and your own wage, payroll burden, disposal, equipment, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into crew hours and a price for this visit -- the arithmetic a flat per-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a home service company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this gutter cleaning visit cost, before you offer it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — lawn care, cleaning, HVAC, plumbing and general contracting among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Jobber's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling, invoicing and collecting payment for a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a gutter cleaning visit should cost from linear feet, stories, pitch, guards, debris and downspouts before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a client list, dispatch a crew across a season, or collect a payment. It takes a house's gutter runs — each one's linear feet, story, pitch, guard type, debris and downspout count — plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, travel and setup, disposal, equipment, overhead and a minimum stop charge, and turns that into the visit price, the walk-away floor, the price per linear foot, the effective crew hourly rate and an optional spring-and-fall contract total — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Jobber?

They do different jobs, and a gutter cleaning business of any size will likely end up touching both. Jobber is a field service management platform used across home service trades to run client management and quoting, scheduling and dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a house's gutter runs — each one's linear feet, stories, pitch, guards, debris and downspouts — plus loaded crew wage, travel, disposal, equipment, overhead and a minimum stop charge, and turns that into the visit price, the walk-away floor, the price per linear foot and an optional spring-and-fall contract total, before you have quoted anything. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A company already scheduling crews, invoicing customers and taking payments across many jobs is better served by Jobber or a comparable field service platform; a contractor who needs an instant, private answer to what one gutter cleaning visit should cost before it is offered is in the right place here.
